red.focus: Recognize injury as a legal and historical category
red.summary: Explore how an early legal text described injury through bodily damage, property and social status. Learn why harm mattered to the law even when people disagreed about a fair response.
checklist: I can distinguish injury from a prescribed penalty
I can recognize status differences in ancient remedies
I can analyze what a judgment reveals and conceals

sections.title: One Injury, Several Legal Responses
sections.body_md: The Babylonian collection associated with Hammurabi includes judgments about bodily injury and property loss. The prescribed response could depend on who injured whom and the social standing of the people involved. This teaches two things at once: the legal order took some injuries seriously, and it did not treat all injured persons as equivalent. Do not assume that an ancient reference to bodily retaliation states a complete general theory of criminal punishment. Read the condition, social category and prescribed consequence together.

Do not assume that an ancient reference to bodily retaliation states a complete general theory of criminal punishment. Read the condition, social category and prescribed consequence together.

sections.title: The Harm Is Not the Sentence
sections.body_md: If a person's eye is injured, the bodily harm is a factual event. Whether the response is payment, retaliation or another consequence is a separate legal choice. Ancient judgments sometimes connected particular injuries with fixed consequences to represent proportionality or social order. The modern reader may criticize those measures, but must first understand their historical function. A historian therefore separates the injury suffered, the legal interest recognized, the party entitled to complain, and the institution empowered to respond.

sections.title: Reading Evidence Responsibly
sections.body_md: A royal collection of judgments is powerful evidence for official views of harm. It does not tell us how every dispute ended or whether the prescriptions were uniformly enforced. We also know less about people whose experiences were not recorded in surviving texts. Responsible legal history resists claiming too much. When comparing an ancient provision with today's law, use the source to identify the legal category and consequence, then look for additional evidence of procedure and lived experience.

yellow.focus: Understand Roman injury concepts and private redress
yellow.summary: Move from fixed ancient judgments to Roman categories of personal and property wrongs. Study why naming an injury in law depended on the available action and the protected interest.
checklist: I can explain what a delictual wrong means historically
I can distinguish private injury claims from public penalties
I can recognize the importance of a procedural action

sections.title: From Harm to an Action
sections.body_md: Roman legal thought developed distinct actions for wrongs involving personal injury, property and other recognized interests. The word delict refers to a category of private-law wrongs, though its content changed across periods. A person might suffer a factual loss yet lack the action needed to obtain a remedy. The legal historian must not assume that every serious moral injury appeared as a general claim. What mattered was the protected interest, available procedural form and legal status of the parties.

The word delict refers to a category of private-law wrongs, though its content changed across periods. A person might suffer a factual loss yet lack the action needed to obtain a remedy. The legal historian must not assume that every serious moral injury appeared as a general claim. What mattered was the protected interest, available procedural form and legal status of the parties.

sections.title: Damnum and the Protected Interest
sections.body_md: Roman discussion of damage to property, including rules associated with the Lex Aquilia, influenced later legal reasoning about wrongful loss. Yet a modern negligence claim cannot simply be read back into a Roman statute. Jurists debated the kinds of conduct and injury the rules encompassed, while procedures and remedies evolved. The historically accurate question is not whether Rome invented every modern tort, but how specific legal actions helped refine ideas of damage, responsibility and compensation.

sections.title: Public and Private Responses
sections.body_md: A public offense may threaten the political order; a private wrong may create a claim between identified persons. Roman arrangements did not always match today's civil-criminal boundary. The same conduct could implicate more than one interest, and remedies could have penal features even when pursued privately. Students must therefore identify the legal forum and type of action before translating a Roman term into modern language. Historical precision prevents a familiar label from concealing a different institutional design.

orange.focus: Explain how common-law forms shaped recognized harms
orange.summary: Trace how forms of action and evolving common-law pleading affected what counted as a legal wrong. See why procedure could determine the practical meaning of harm long before broad modern doctrines emerged.
checklist: I can distinguish trespass from action on the case historically
I can recognize how forms of action influenced substance
I can explain why legal categories changed as institutions changed

sections.title: A Writ Could Define the Path
sections.body_md: In medieval and early modern English common law, litigants often had to bring claims within recognized writs and forms of action. Trespass developed around certain direct interferences; action on the case gradually supplied routes for other fact patterns. Their historical boundaries shifted and cannot be reduced to one timeless formula. A wrong without an available procedural path might be difficult to remedy. That is why legal historians examine court procedure when asking what injuries a legal order truly protected.

sections.title: From Forms to General Principles
sections.body_md: Over centuries, common-law pleading and judicial reasoning increasingly reorganized questions of injury, duty and causation. Reforms later reduced the formal dominance of older writ categories, but traces remain in substantive doctrines. The change did not happen overnight and should not be described as a simple replacement of primitive law with modern fairness. Each procedural innovation could expand some claims and exclude others. The analytical lesson is that a legal system's definition of harm develops alongside its mechanisms for hearing people.

sections.title: The Missing Claimant
sections.body_md: Legal records frequently preserve the disputes that reached institutions able to write and retain documents. Poorer people, women and marginalized groups may be underrepresented in surviving reports for many reasons. A history of reported actions is therefore not necessarily a complete history of harm. When evaluating how protective a system was, ask who could afford proceedings, whose testimony was heard and whether the recognized interests fit people's lived injuries. Institutional access belongs within the history of substantive law.

black.focus: Analyze systemic injury beyond the individual lawsuit
black.summary: Examine how industrial, environmental and digital harms challenge legal categories built for distinct people and isolated events. Evaluate whether a system that recognizes only individualized injuries can respond adequately to collective risks.
checklist: I can differentiate individual and systemic injuries
I can analyze evidentiary gaps in diffuse harms
I can defend reforms without treating causation as optional

sections.title: Harm Changes With Social Organization
sections.body_md: Industrial pollution, unsafe workplaces and mass-market products exposed injuries involving many people, long time periods and uncertain sources. Modern environmental risks and large data systems create similar structural problems. Traditional bilateral litigation can still be valuable, but its proof and remedy requirements may not fit every collective injury. Historical analysis should track how institutions adapted through regulation, insurance, group litigation and public enforcement in different jurisdictions. Change in the pattern of harm can require change in legal response.

sections.title: The Invisible Victim
sections.body_md: Some harms are difficult to see in a single case: cumulative exposure, discriminatory patterns or information asymmetry may emerge only through broader evidence. Statistical associations can identify problems but do not automatically prove a defendant's liability to a particular claimant. A doctoral student must distinguish the existence of a population-level risk, the harm to an identified person and the legal rule assigning responsibility. Those distinctions protect both victims seeking meaningful relief and defendants against unsupported attribution.

sections.title: A Historic Test of Justice
sections.body_md: Ask whether a legal system measures injury only by losses it already knows how to remedy. If so, important harms may become invisible because the doctrine was designed for another age. A reform proposal should identify the social interest, establish reliable proof, address the risk of false attribution and choose an institution capable of effective enforcement. The aim is not unlimited liability. It is an honest legal vocabulary that can recognize new harms while preserving fair limits on coercive power.
